Additional experiments on Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB with non-hierarchical MPAD found that using an undirected graph improves Reuters but has the opposite effect on Polarity and IMDB.
Additional experiments on Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB with non-hierarchical MPAD found that varying message passing iterations from 1 to 4 improves performance with more iterations.
Additional experiments on Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB with non-hierarchical MPAD found that removing the master node deteriorates performance across all datasets.
Additional experiments on Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB with non-hierarchical MPAD found that using sum instead of mean decreases performance everywhere.

Additional experiments on Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB with non-hierarchical MPAD found that replacing the GRU combine function with the identity function makes performance always suffer except on Reuters.
Because Reuters is a topic classification task while Polarity and IMDB are sentiment analysis tasks, undirected edges help Reuters but hurt sentiment tasks where modeling word order is crucial.
BIBREF53 requires computing PMI for every word pair in the vocabulary, while MPAD complexity does not depend on vocabulary size, avoiding a limitation on datasets with very large vocabularies.

The proposed user-aware encoder-decoder with attention fusion addresses existing approaches' failure to handle personal preference and incomplete recipe details by attending over user profiles learned from previously consumed recipes.
Quantitative perplexity, user-ranking, and qualitative analyses support the claim that personalized models generate high-quality and specific recipes that align with historical user preferences.
The released dataset of 180K+ recipes and 700K+ user reviews is the filtered Food.com dataset obtained by discarding users with fewer than 4 reviews.
The Prior Name model uses averages of name-token embeddings from the k-most recent prior recipes, and it achieves the best UMA and MRR by a large margin.
The Prior Tech model's technique preference vector is built from techniques seen in R^+_u using the manually constructed list of 58 cooking techniques.
Under sequential leave-one-out evaluation on recipes not in the training set, all personalized models outperform baseline in BPE perplexity, with Prior Name performing the best.
The human evaluation used partial recipe specifications with name and 3-5 key ingredients, matching the experimental setting that provides the first 3-5 ingredients listed in each recipe.

Human evaluators preferred personalized model outputs to baseline 63% of the time in comparisons where one recipe came from the baseline encoder-decoder model and one from Prior Tech, Prior Name, or Prior Recipe.

The conclusion that personalized generative models produce coherent recipes preferred by human evaluators is supported by recipe-level coherence scores of 1.78-1.82 surpassing the baseline at 1.77 and 63% human preference.
The IG-based Attribution method is evaluated by BLEU decrease under perturbations and consistently outperforms Content, Frequency, Attention, and Random across three perturbations.
Because Attention simulates SOCRAT and Attribution beats Attention by around 1.0+ BLEU, the gradient-based approach empirically supports its claimed superiority over the best black-box method.
Under Mask perturbation with five operations, Attribution reduces BLEU to around half the original score across English⇒French, English⇒Japanese, and reverse directions using Transformer.
The RNN-Search validation shows Attribution still outperforms Attention and Random, while RNN-Search is less robust than Transformer with 64% versus 55% BLEU decrease.

The finding that nouns matter for Chinese⇒English while prepositions matter for English-French and -Japanese supports the design principle that language characteristics should guide NMT architectures.
The experiments use WMT17 Chinese-English, WMT14 English-French, and WAT17 English-Japanese datasets with Transformer and RNN-Search trained for 100k steps.

Punctuation is important on English⇒Japanese translation and more important on Japanese⇒English, supporting the conclusion that syntactic distribution with word importance is language-pair related instead of the direction.
The gradient-based method is superior to several black-box methods in estimating word importance, and detected unimportant words are possibly under-translated.
Important words are of distinct syntactic categories on different language pairs, supporting the proposal that language-specific inductive bias should be incorporated into the model design.

One-to-many fertility is consistently more important on all three language pairs, and reverse directions show one-to-many fertility is more important, further confirming the generality of experimental findings.

Null-aligned words receive much less attention on three language pairs, and reverse directions show null-aligned fertility is less important, further confirming the generality of experimental findings.

PolyResponse addresses the manual ontology design and scarce annotated in-domain data challenges by using non-generative response retrieval trained on hundreds of millions of Reddit conversations with implicit semantics.

Because PolyResponse relies on retrieval-based design, it avoids engineering a structured ontology and dedicated decision-making policy modules that explicit-semantics task-oriented dialogue systems require.
The PolyResponse ranking model scores conversational replies and images by scaled cosine similarity between context encodings and candidate text or photo encodings.
The text encoder trained on more than 727M Reddit context-reply pairs produces the 512-dimensional $h_c$ and $h_r$ representations used by the PolyResponse similarity scoring.
The photo encoder learned on around 200K Yelp photos and captions enables the system to score photos by whether their captions would be good responses to the current context.
At inference, PolyResponse uses the Yelp dataset as the candidate pool and finds relevant text and photo responses by nearest-neighbour search over pre-computed $h_r$ and $h_p$ vectors.

The one-shot ranking model is extended into restaurant-browsing dialogue flow by repeatedly ranking responses, aggregating their probability scores per restaurant, and narrowing the relevant restaurant set $R$.
When the narrowing dialogue flow reaches only one relevant restaurant, PolyResponse displays the top $N$ responses and relevant photos, implementing the multi-modal response capability.
The 8-language PolyResponse restaurant search is enabled by a translate-to-source approach that translates foreign response pools and user utterances into English for the English-trained encodings.
The need to reset $R$ and transfer to slot-based table booking is handled by two binary intent classifiers using the already-computed 512-dimensional $h_c$ vector.

Because sequential neural models need massive unlabeled conversational data while forecasting tasks have at most a few thousands labeled examples, CRAFT uses pre-training on unlabeled data before fine-tuning.
CRAFT's HRED context encoder supplies the context encoding used by the predictor, enabling the model to capture relations between comments that Cumulative BoW fails to account for.
The CMV dataset's lack of post-hoc annotation limits controls, yet its 6,842 conversations are used to evaluate CRAFT against fixed-window and online baselines.
The evaluation counts a forecast as a true positive only if triggered before derailment, which operationalizes the goal of giving moderators time to intervene before harm.
Prior forecasting work's hand-crafted features from fixed-length windows leave the unknown-horizon problem unaddressed, while CRAFT processes comments and their relations online.
The Wikipedia dataset's civil comments before personal attacks force models to capture conversational dynamics, aligning with CRAFT's need to model relations between comments.
CRAFT's design capacity to learn an order-sensitive representation of conversational context is empirically supported by the prefix-shuffling experiment.
The model that processes comments as they happen and takes the full conversational context into account is CRAFT, whose architecture follow-up work could adapt.
Open questions about what human moderators actually desire from an early-warning system motivate a user study of a prototype system with actual moderators.
The single-label limitation of the present work conflicts with the possibility that a conversation could get back on track or suffer a repeat occurrence of antisocial behavior.
Because contextualised models cannot be evaluated on static tasks, the authors used WSD with Senseval-3 for English and RUSSE'18 for Russian to compare ELMo trained before and after lemmatization.
The authors' ELMo models trained on corpora tokenized and lemmatized with UDPipe were evaluated on WSD datasets pre-processed the same way, producing lemmatized and non-lemmatized versions.
The widely believed assumption that lemmatization is unnecessary is contradicted for Russian by ELMo (target) on lemmas outperforming ELMo on tokens in WSD.
The Russian lemma-based improvement is mostly driven by 3 of 18 words, qualifying the claim that lemmatization yields small but consistent improvements in the WSD task.
The feature-extraction setup using single target word vectors from the ELMo top layer led the authors to discuss only that mode after averaging was not beneficial for WSD with ELMo.
The MLP classifier with 200-neurons hidden layer yielding essentially the same results as simple logistic regression supports the claim that the findings are not classifier-dependent.

TCEN addresses the common pre-training practice's subnet waste, role mismatch and non-pre-trained attention issues by reusing all subnets, keeping roles consistent, and pre-training the attention module.
Because the common practice initializes ST with only the ASR encoder and MT decoder, the MT encoder's valuable semantic information cannot be inherited by the final ST system.
TCEN's tandem ASR encoder and MT encoder disentangle acoustic and linguistic feature extraction, addressing the role mismatch caused by the speech encoder's changing roles.
TCEN reuses the pre-trained MT attention module in ST, overcoming the prior limitation that the ST attention module did not benefit from pre-training.

Because speech encoder output length is proportional to input frame length and much longer than word embeddings, lengthening MT source sentences with repetitions and blank tokens targets length inconsistency.
TCEN is evaluated on the IWSLT18 speech translation benchmark and is significantly better than previous methods by 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU scores for subword-level and character-level decoding.
The CTC-based ASR pre-training of enc_s on dataset A enables TCEN to avoid an ASR decoder while still reading acoustic features into the source language space.
TCEN's pre-training uses CTC objective for enc_s on dataset A and MT dataset M for enc_t and dec, then fine-tuning jointly updates ASR, MT, and ST tasks.
TCEN is evaluated on IWSLT18 speech translation task using lowercase BLEU, with tst2010, tst2013, tst2014, tst2015 as test sets.
The ASR model used for encoder pre-training is trained on ST-TED and TED-LIUM2, which together provide 272 hours and 207 hours of English speech.
The MT model used for decoder pre-training is first trained on WMT data, corresponding to WMT2018 out-of-domain training data with 41M sentence pairs.
The MT model used for decoder pre-training is fine-tuned on in-domain data consisting of ST-TED and WIT3 transcription and translation pairs with 130k and 200k sentence pairs.
The corpus’s information on text structure, typography, and images is empirically supported by battisti-2019, who found structural features predictive of simplified German text difficulty.

Because automatic text simplification via machine translation needs sentence-level parallel corpora, the corpus’s missing sentence alignments limit its parallel documents for neural machine translation.
The proposed CATS tool addresses the missing sentence alignments required for using the corpus’s parallel documents in machine translation.
The corpus extends the only previously available simplified German corpus by adding more parallel data, monolingual-only data, and information on text structure, typography, and images.
The corpus’s 52 websites and 233 PDFs with explicit language level labels enable automatic readability assessment and graded automatic text simplification experiments.

The corpus’s parallel data supports both rule-based text simplification and data-driven machine translation, while its monolingual-only data can yield additional synthetic parallel data via back-translation.
The corpus’s novel text structure, typography, and image information required extending TCF with token attributes, textstructure textspans, and separate images and fonts layers.
The corpus’s PDFs and webpages were processed so that HTML and TETML files supplied metadata, with TETML produced by the PDFlib Text and Image Extraction Toolkit (TET).
The corpus addresses scarce German research by providing data for automatic readability assessment and automatic text simplification of German, tasks that rely on systematically prepared corpora.
RQ2 [Political Inclination] is supported by party name mentions and famous political handle mentions testifying that people display political inclination via profile attributes.
RQ3 [Behavior Contagion] is evidenced by Narendra Modi removing Chowkidar on 23rd May and the majority of set S removing it too.
RQ4 [Topic Modelling] is answered by topic modelling showing Chowkidar movement users were most likely Narendra Modi supporters and mostly discussed political topics on Twitter.
For the same 9 snapshots, 54.9% of set P made at least one profile change while only 3% of set S made any changes.
Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) similarity analysis shows nearly 80% of set S made more significant Display Name changes than political handles.
The regular expression query over Chowkidar variants found 2,60,607 display-name instances, supporting the claim that the Chowkidar movement was very widespread.

The “Chowkidar movement” is treated as inorganic behavior contagion because followers added chowkidar to profile attributes after @narendramodi did, consistent with opinion leaders helping followers adopt behavior.
The paper’s study of profile attribute changes during #LokSabhaElectios2019 extends prior work that says profile attributes can represent social movement at macro-level.

The paper’s investigation of profile attribute changes similar or different from influential leaders addresses the literature claim that opinion leaders on social media platforms help adoption of behavior by followers easily.
The finding that about $80\%$ changes made by followers was related to #LokSabhaElectios2019 supports the claim that other profile changes can be triggered by certain events.
The paper’s focus on 5 major attributes, including Profile Name, Username, Description, Profile Image, and Location, broadens previous studies’ extensive focus on change in username attribute.
Back-translation was applied to tackle the imbalance between the training, validation and test sets by increasing indirect and physical harassment tweets.
The Projected Layer is the one-layer MLP with tanh and 128 hidden units, and its addition significantly enhanced performance in most cases.
The competition dataset's two tasks correspond to the four scores produced by each model: harassment language, indirect, physical and sexual harassment language.
The four self-attentions in the model architecture implement the MultiAttentionRNN model's four attentions, one for each category.
The Embedding Layer is initialized using pre-trained word embeddings of dimension 200 from Twitter data that have 27B tokens.
The paper's focus on different types of online harassment addresses the limitation that previous broad sexism and racism categories undermined other harassment types.
The attention mechanism replaces the LR Layer's use of $h_{k}$ with $h_{sum}$, whose weights $\alpha _{t}$ come from the attention mechanism presented in BIBREF9.
CJFA predicts temporal context Y from a single centre segment X and significantly outperforms the VAE baseline and CJFS in phone classification and speaker recognition.
The proposed CJFS and CJFA extend the re-implemented VAE baseline that gave 72.0% phone classification accuracy, close to the published 72.2% VAE baseline.
The RM corpus augmented TIMIT only for embedding training while labelled data remained the same, and classification tasks still benefited from the additional data.
The contextual models were evaluated on TIMIT with 80 dimensional Mel-scale filter bank coefficients and a 30-frame window, where CJFA obtained significantly better phone classification accuracy.
Unlike earlier article-level propaganda work whose labels used distant supervision and introduced noise, the shared task corpus was annotated by professional annotators.
Task 11 at SemEval 2020 follows up the shared task by splitting FLC's span detection and technique identification into binary sequence labeling and multi-class classification.
Because privacy policies are intended for the general public, PrivacyQA elicits questions from crowdworkers rather than individuals with legal expertise.
The extractive sentence selection task uses expert-identified relevant evidence within privacy policies as gold-reference sentences for sentence-level F1.
BERT's 124 answerability mistakes on the test set support the claim that a more nuanced understanding of answerability might improve model performance.
The 573 unanswerable questions are not homogeneous because experts identified incomprehensibility, relevance, ill-formedness, silence and atypicality as factors.
The atypicality category corresponds closely to 12% of sampled natural unanswerable questions unlikely to ever contain an answer on Wikipedia.
Because CE or MLE handles neither the training-test discrepancy nor easy-negative dominance, the paper replaces CE loss with dice loss or Tversky index and adds dynamic weight adjusting.
The proposed DSC loss is evaluated on three Chinese POS datasets, CTB5, CTB6 and UD1.4, and outperforms BERT-tagger by +1.86, +1.80 and +2.19 F1.
The dynamic weight adjusting strategy is inspired by focal loss, which down-weights well-classified examples, and is used to alleviate easy-negative dominance.
Baselines optimized with standard cross-entropy are compared against the proposed DSC loss, which outperforms BERT-tagger by +1.86, +1.80 and +2.19 F1 on POS datasets.
DSC loss improves F1 on the imbalanced PI datasets MRPC and QQP by +0.58 and +0.73, respectively.
The F1-oriented dice loss slightly degrades accuracy on SST-5 and SST-2, where BERT with CE achieves 55.57 and 94.9.
The conclusion that dice loss boosts paraphrase identification is evidenced by DSC improving F1 by +0.58 for MRPC and +0.73 for QQP.
The proposed DSC loss improves MRC results with BERT and XLNet, the backbones described as treating NER as tagging and enabling bidirectional contexts.
DSC loss is complementary to model structures because it further improves MRC performance even when XLNet outperforms BERT by a huge margin.
The severe data imbalance issue addressed by dice loss is instantiated by MRPC's 68% positive, 32% negative classes and QQP's 37% positive, 63% negative classes.
The conclusion that dice loss boosts machine reading comprehension is evidenced by DSC outperforming XLNet by +1.25 F1 and +0.84 EM on SQuADv1.1.
The instability of naively weighting and searching over $\lambda $ motivates the constrained objective, which is 11.73% more accurate at a 53.38% retention rate.
The constrained objective minimizes expected cost under $\epsilon $ constraints and results in more efficient schemes than the linear objective at every accuracy level.
Because efficiency is quantified by retention rate, the constrained model's 52.16% accuracy improvement at a 77.37% retention rate is an efficiency-accuracy tradeoff gain over Unif.
The proposed restriction of keywords to subsequences is implemented by the stochastic encoder $q_{\alpha }(z\mid x)$ keeping a subset of tokens.
The claim that humans save nearly 50% of time is supported by users spending $3.86$ seconds typing keywords compared to $5.76$ seconds for full sentences.
In the AMT user study, users shown the top three suggestions marked one of the top 3 semantically equivalent $90.11$% of the time.
The linear objective's slight $\lambda $ changes causing degenerate schemes explains why it requires careful tuning.
The new objective optimizes communication efficiency under an accuracy constraint, while $\epsilon $ in Eq (DISPLAY_FORM6) directly controls maximum reconstruction error.
The framework trained on 500K randomly sampled sentences from Yelp reviews produced communication schemes 52.16% more accurate than rule-based baselines when specifying 77.37% of sentences.
The proposed hierarchical naive Bayesian and lexicon based classifier for 15-20 character texts was evaluated on NCHLT BIBREF7, DSL 2015 BIBREF19 and DSL 2017 BIBREF1 datasets.
The proposed algorithm beat the other methods on three existing datasets, but its performance is dependent on the support of the lexicon.
The lexicon based classifier's high-confidence rule uses a one-word margin over second place, while its design trades higher precision for lower recall.
The proposed classifier addresses the difficulty of distinguishing similar Nguni and Sotho languages by using a lexicon based classifier within those groups.
The proposed algorithm targets short texts of 15-20 characters, while LID of short texts and similar languages remains a difficult problem.
The stacked classifier was compared with three public LID implementations and four other algorithms using the NCHLT BIBREF7, DSL 2015 BIBREF19 and DSL 2017 BIBREF1 datasets.
The proposed algorithm's dependence on lexicon support is evidenced by the 50% training token dropout lexicon listed to show the impact of lexicon support on accuracy.

The conclusion that existing publicly available ELMo embeddings are inadequate is supported by ELMoForManyLangs Latvian embeddings performing significantly worse than EMBEDDIA ELMo Latvian model on all word analogy categories.

The conclusion that training set size importantly affects embedding quality is supported by 20-million token corpora being too small and a few hundred million tokens being sufficiently large for word analogy.
The conclusion that newly produced contextual embeddings produce substantially better results than fastText is supported by ELMo improving NER results on all EMBEDDIA languages except Slovenian.
The NER evaluation of produced ELMo models used Macro F1 score after averaging the three ELMo layer vectors for each token.
The Latvian dataset consists only of the Latvian portion of the CoNLL 2017 corpus, making Latvian the only language where EMBEDDIA ELMo and ELMoForManyLangs used exactly the same corpora.

The human-AI loop approach addresses the challenging keyword expectation estimation and keyword informativeness constraint by jointly discovering informative keywords and estimating their expectations.
The unified probabilistic model resolves the inter-dependency between expectation inference and model training by inferring keyword expectation and performing model training simultaneously.
Because AUC better characterizes discriminative power under dataset imbalance, the reported average of 24.3% AUC improvement is evaluated with the more informative metric.

The keyword discovery method selects microposts with the highest disagreement between model predictions and keyword-specific expectation, then crowd workers identify the most frequent keyword for the following iteration.

The unified probabilistic model connects expectation inference with model training by using keyword-specific expectation both as a class prior for crowd labels and as a regularization term for model training.

Because ground truth labels of crowd-annotated microposts are unknown, the learning algorithm uses an E-step to infer them and an M-step to update crowd reliability, keyword expectation, and target model parameters.
The human-AI loop approach configured to start each iteration with 1 new keyword discovered in the previous iteration improves LR by 5.17% Accuracy and 18.38% AUC on average.
The human-AI loop approach configured to start each iteration with 1 new keyword discovered in the previous iteration improves MLP by 10.71% Accuracy and 30.27% AUC on average.
The conclusion that the approach is particularly useful for semantically complex events is supported by its 52.58% AUC advantage over QE on PoliticianDeath.
The conclusion that the approach significantly outperforms the state of the art is supported by its average 4.62% and 52.58% AUC gains over QE on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath.
The cost-effectiveness conclusion is supported by the same-cost comparison where additional micropost labels increase AUC by 0.87% for CyberAttack and 1.06% for PoliticianDeath.
The conclusion's expectation inference component is supported by the comparison where the method improves majority voting by 0.4% and 1.19% AUC on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath.
The conclusion's keyword discovery component is supported by the comparison where the approach outperforms QE by an average of 4.62% and 52.58% AUC on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath.
The conclusion's claim about semantically complex events is supported by PoliticianDeath microposts being semantically more complex than CyberAttack microposts and the 52.58% AUC gain over QE.
The proposed cross-lingual pre-training based transfer approach addresses the language space mismatch problem that causes zero-shot translation failure in transfer learning.
BRLM uses source↔pivot bilingual data to obtain a universal encoder, enabling the pivot→target parent model to translate source sentences into target sentences directly.
The approach is evaluated with BLEU on Europarl and MultiUN, and its approaches consistently outperform pivoting, MNMT, and cross-lingual transfer without pretraining.
Pivoting requires doubled decoding time and suffers from error propagation, while the proposed approaches use one encoder-decoder model and are more efficient than pivoting.
The pretraining phase builds a cross-lingual encoder shared by source and pivot languages, addressing the key difficulty of making universal encoder representations language invariant.

On Europarl, English acts as the pivot language, and the shared encoder trained on large-scale monolingual data and parallel data between multiple languages improves supervised pivot→target performance.
The paper's aim of building language invariant representation is supported by MLM+BRLM-SA showing stable sentence-pair representations and better word-level representation alignment.
Because all freezing experiments are based on MLM+BRLM-SA, freezing the first four layers balances pre-training and fine-tuning for the best-performing proposed approach.
The conclusion that the approaches manifest language invariance in sentence level and word level neural representations is jointly evidenced by sentence-pair and aligned-word analyses.

PitchNet addresses BIBREF0's difficulty on learning joint representation of phonetic and pitch representation by adding an adversarially trained pitch regression network and extracted pitch input to the decoder.
The pitch regression loss makes the whole model obtain pitch information from $p(s^j)$, which is the extracted pitch fed into the decoder after linear interpolation.
PitchNet's claim of greatly improving converted voice quality is supported by Mean Opinion Score (MOS) results where naturalness and similarity are both higher than the other two ones.
PitchNet's flexible pitch manipulation is evidenced by multiplying input pitch by 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 and observing output pitch changes significantly along with input pitch.
The pitch regression network that separates pitch information out of the latent space is trained adversarially using $\mathcal {L}_{ad}$ while the whole model uses $\mathcal {L}_{total}$.
Because only reconstruction loss is not enough to learn conversion, PitchNet adds singer classification loss and pitch regression loss adversarially to the reconstruction loss.

The conclusion that PitchNet outperforms the existing unsupervised singing voice conversion method is supported by comparisons against USVC(our) using automatic evaluation score and human evaluation score.
The lack of large-scale publicly available databases for text-dependent speaker recognition motivated collecting DeepMine, whose final cleaned-up version is publicly available for everybody.
DeepMine addresses the Persian ASR data gap by providing Part3 for Persian read speech recognition with a 450-hour train-set.
The i-vector based method applied to the Persian portion of Part1 was evaluated on the 100-spk with 3-session enrollment (3-sess) main evaluation condition.
The most difficult trials in Table TABREF23 combine “NN” target trials and “YY” non-target trials, where channel effects caused severe degradation.
Because 297 respondents could not read English, English Part1 recordings were limited to speakers who can read English, yielding fewer speakers in each English set than Persian.
Part3 is the last part with word- and phoneme-level transcription and can serve both text-independent speaker verification and large vocabulary speech recognition in Persian.

The speech recognition experiments on Part3 with the Kaldi toolkit are the baseline speech recognition experiments described as using conventional HMM-based methods and a state-of-the-art deep neural network based method.
The claim that the created database can train well performing and practically usable Persian ASR models is supported by speech recognition experiments on Part3 using the Kaldi toolkit.
The proposed hierarchical encoder addresses linearization and arbitrary ordering limitations by using a two-level architecture with Transformer encoders and hierarchical attention.
The proposed architecture is generally better on qualitative metrics that estimate the ability to integrate elements from the table in descriptions.
The Transformer encoder is introduced to avoid arbitrary ordering assumptions that significantly impact learning performance in RNN encoders.
The two-level architecture matches the notation where an entity is a set of unordered records and a data-structure is an unordered set of entities.
The data-structure representation z computed by the high-level encoder initializes the two-layers LSTM network with a copy mechanism.
Traditional Hierarchical Attention implements the hierarchical context by attending first to entities and then to records belonging to those entities.
Key-guided Hierarchical Attention tests the intuition that once an entity is chosen, only the type of records is important by computing beta scores from key embeddings.

Hierarchical-k, which computes attention over records only on record key representations, performs slightly better in all metrics excepted CS-R% than Hierarchical-kv, which uses the full record encoding.
Flat uses a Transformer instead of an RNN and obtains a significant higher BLEU score (16.7 vs. 14.5) than Wiseman, which uses bi-LSTM.
The hierarchical models outperform Li and Puduppully-plan, whose delayed copy mechanism and two-step plan generation place structure prediction in the decoder.

The hierarchical encoder leverages structure and has strong synergy with hierarchical attention, while the scenarios rely on 14 millions parameters compared to all baselines ranging from 23 to 45 millions.

The comparative analysis of BERT, XLNet and RoBERTa on speculation detection and scope resolution uses the Khandelwal and Sawant (BIBREF12) methodology modified to support experimentation with multiple models.
The single dataset training approach that outperforms all existing systems on speculation detection and scope resolution reports results as an average of 5 runs of the model.
The inter-dataset scores used to test generalizability show BF gets the best results when trained on BA, while BF has 2670 sentences and BA has 11871 sentences.
Jointly training on multiple datasets, which improves performance over single dataset training on most datasets, reports results as an average of 3 runs of the model.
The observation that XLNet consistently outperforms RoBERTa on speculation detection and scope resolution is confirmed by applying the 2 models to negation detection and scope resolution.
State-of-the-art results on three of four datasets on the negation scope resolution task correspond to BF, BA and SFU datasets.
The word ‘tomorrow' split into 3 tokens, ‘tom', ‘##or' and ‘##row', is handled by First Token using the output vector corresponding to ‘tom'.
For fair comparison across BERT, XLNet and RoBERTa, only the tokenizer and the model are changed while the same hyperparameters are used for the entire architecture for all 3 models.
RKS applied to Fasttext features reached 99.53% maximum accuracy, exceeding the 81.16% maximum accuracy from classical machine learning algorithms using fasttext features.
RKS applied to Google universal encoder features reached 90.58% maximum accuracy, exceeding the 82.44% and 82.56% maximum accuracies from classical machine learning algorithms using those features.
The paper's comparative analysis targets Sub-task A, whose goal was to discriminate offensive and not-offensive twitter posts.
The proposed RKS approach is compared against Case 1 & 2 baseline approaches, and the conclusion states that RKS approach improved the results.
The proposed methodology addresses the extremely large action space by using Go-Explore to extract high reward trajectories and then training a Seq2Seq model on them.
The Seq2Seq policy maps observations to actions by encoding observation tokens and decoding action tokens, matching the POMDP definitions of observations and actions as token sequences.
CookingWorld is used to evaluate generalization because CoinCollector has a very limited action space while CookingWorld has 4,440 games with 222 different levels of difficulty.
The Zero-Shot setting tests the stronger generalization claimed for training a Seq2Seq model on Go-Explore trajectories by evaluating on unseen test games.
DRRN corresponds to the second reinforcement learning approach because it learns one Q-function that scores admissible actions rather than generating actions token by token.
The hardest CookingWorld games require a very long sequence of actions, and most lost games for Go-Explore Seq2Seq are in the hardest set.
On the 1,000-tweet dataset, crowdworkers reached 74.7% CCR for entity-level sentiment analysis, while Rosette Text Analytics, Google Cloud, and TensiStrength reached 31.7%, 43.2%, and 44.2%.

The baseline performance that any new machine learning system for political tweet analysis would compete against was measured as 31.7% for Rosette Text Analytics, 43.2% for Google Cloud, and 44.2% for TensiStrength.
The 3-scale rating of "negative," "neutral," and "positive" corresponds to the three-class sentiment analysis problem whose CCR was 74.7% for crowdworkers.
The groundtruth labels considered from experts in political communication contain 210 positive sentiments, 521 neutral sentiments, and 305 negative sentiments to the candidates.
RAMEN is the name of the bilingual LMs produced by the fast adaptation method that obtains a bilingual BERT$_{\textsc {base}}$ within a day using one Tesla V100 16GB GPU.
The proposed approach addresses the difficulty of translating English pre-training advancements to non-English languages by transferring an existing English pre-trained model to other languages.
RAMEN$_{\textsc {base}}$+BERT trained with monolingual only is the fairest comparison with mBERT and slightly outperforms mBERT by 1.9 points on average on XNLI.
RAMEN is evaluated on XNLI and dependency parsing, which use XNLI dataset BIBREF9 and Universal Dependencies v2.4 BIBREF21 respectively.
RAMEN's bilingual LM has two separate embedding layers and output layers with a shared encoder, and the encoder parameters are updated to learn target-language syntactic aspects.
RAMEN$_{\textsc {base}}$ is tuned for 175,000 updates and each RAMEN$_{\textsc {base}}$ model is trained within a day on a single Tesla V100 16GB GPU.
The supervised UD evaluation provides evidence for the conclusion that RAMEN is a powerful feature extractor in supervised dependency parsing.
RAMEN models tuned on English for zero-shot cross-lingual tasks were also evaluated as feature extractors for supervised dependency parsing on UD datasets.

French's 50.3 LAS without tuning the English encoder and Arabic and Hindi's 4.2 and 6.4 points using the SVO encoder support the claim that language similarities have more impact on transferring syntax than semantics.
The conclusion that RAMEN is a powerful feature extractor in supervised dependency parsing is supported by RAMEN$_{\textsc {large}}$+RoBERTa with 24 Transformer layers obtaining the best LAS results.
Integrating boundary assembling into the LSTM-CRF pipeline yields a 2% absolute improvement on overall F1 score over current state-of-the-art methods on the Sina Weibo training and test datasets.
Boundary assembling addresses Chinese word segmentation errors that can cause cascading failure in NER by preserving sense groups and improving downstream NER results.
The boundary assembling strategy reduces the influence of different segmentation criteria and finds named entities with long word length, addressing two Chinese word segmentation challenges.

The computational linguistic framework applies lexical correlates of negative evaluations, denial of agency, moral disgust, and non-human metaphors to changing representations of LGBTQ groups in the New York Times over three decades.

Because no known large-scale analyses existed and computational linguistic methods enable large-scale study, the framework addresses the need to understand how dehumanizing attitudes evolved over long periods of time.
The framework's comparison of denotationally-similar labels gay and homosexual is supported by word embedding neighbor valence, which can reveal meaning variation between related group labels.
The expectation that homosexual occurs in more dehumanizing contexts than gay is grounded in survey evidence that respondents who read “homosexual” tended to show less support for LGBTQ rights.
Paragraph-level valence analysis uses paragraphs because full articles often focused on topics unrelated to LGBTQ communities and single sentences did not provide enough discussion.
Connotation Frames addresses paragraph-level valence analysis being too coarse by providing writer-perspective scores for the verb's subject and object.
Word embedding neighbor valence addresses the Connotation Frames limitation to SVO triples by using vector space models that represent each unique word in a large corpus.

The diachronic word embedding approach can investigate changing representations of LGBTQ groups in the New York Times over three decades because vector space models trained on corpora from different time periods can capture semantic change.
